cells.tense: Right now you are letting something end because it has finished, not out of avoidance.
cells.act: put it in proportion, not in punishment
cells.ask: If you're settling something with someone, adjust the share until it's fair — give back what's owed you both. Then stop, and don't revisit it to check.
cells.core:
Endings you trust come from the centre here, and you can tell the difference between something that's done and something that hurts. What has finished gets honoured rather than propped up. You're able to say out loud that a thing is over without turning it into a punishment for anyone, least of all yourself.

To keep that, offer one exchange the shape it actually has. If you're settling something with someone, adjust the share until it's fair — give back what's owed you both. Then stop, and don't revisit it to check. It may be an apology owed, or time, or the last word. The balance holds because you stop when it's level, not because you keep score. Let the fair thing rest once it's fair.
cells.sheetLine: You end what has finished without turning it into punishment.
cells.verb: Honouring necessary endings and letting what has finished clear
cells.place: Where you bear what must be borne, and hold form under pressure

cells.tense: You will be reading the next release as liberation before anyone has lived inside what is ending now.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Pick one hard thing you're in and stay with it — the person it touches, or the fact itself. Don't end or fix anything yet.
cells.core:
Endings come fast here, and each one looks like freedom before it has been lived through. An upheaval starts to feel like growth, and the fear underneath gets called release. What's actually needed is the opposite of more clearing: staying in the thing long enough to find out what it is.

So instead of cutting, remain. Pick one hard thing you're in and stay with it — the person it touches, or the fact itself. Don't end or fix anything yet. Contact that outlasts the discomfort is what tells you whether the ending is real or only wanted. Some of it will settle by itself; the part that stays will tell you what it is. The choice will be yours without the hurry.
cells.sheetLine: You call fear liberation and end what hasn't finished.

cells.tense: You keep holding what ended a while back, and you call the holding loyalty.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Find one place your attention is already drawn, and put an hour into moving it one step — a call, a box, a message, a page. One step only.
cells.core:
Here you carry what you've carried a while, and some of it has been over for longer than you'd say. Holding on reads as faithfulness, so nothing gets cleared, and the strength that could bear a real ending keeps bearing a finished one instead. The stagnation looks like loyalty from where you stand, and from outside it looks like standing still.

Don't try to want the ending. Go where the pull already is. Find one place your attention is already drawn, and put an hour into moving it one step — a call, a box, a message, a page. One step only. Momentum comes from the feeling you do have, not from summoning one you don't. The step tells you more than a decision would.

cells.tense: Something is already ending around you, and you carry it without knowing you are.
cells.act: write the order things go in
cells.ask: Write five lines about what is changing near you, worded as what happens next, not what you feel. The last line is what you do about it this month.
cells.core:
Changes are underway close to you, and the bending happens quietly: you attend to the day without noticing that a chapter has already turned. The strength that holds things steady is doing its work, and what it holds is partly gone. Most of the people near you can see it before you can. What you are carrying is real; you are simply the last to know it.

Give it a shape on paper, because shapes reach you where feelings don't. Write five lines about what is changing near you, worded as what happens next, not what you feel. The last line is what you do about it this month. Reading it back, you may find you already knew, and now it has somewhere to stand. Nothing has to be decided tonight; the page will keep it.
cells.sheetLine: Something is ending near you and you carry it unaware.
cells.verb: Honouring necessary endings and letting what has finished clear
cells.place: Where you bear what must be borne, and hold form under pressure

attempts.check: The record does not say what has ended, what the person is holding, or whose imbalance is being corrected. A reader could say the ending is not needed, only hard, and that nothing is dying. The asks survive that: they are small acts of calibration, contact, or structure that help regardless of whether the read is right. The sentence that most serves me is 'clinging to what is dead' — a verdict the seat does not support, so the Too Little cell says only that things continue past their time, not why or since when.
